grammar.name: Stimulative
grammar.explanation: The party/entity/idea/thought/situation or mental state which triggers an unwilled, affective response or is the trigger for an existential states with no tangibly affected patient, e.g., The hammerexemplifies toolship, The man possesses a cat, That book contains poems. Its semantic role is that of STIMULUS.
grammar.guidance: When the stimulus is an instance of musical performance framing attendance at a scheduled event, English often synthesizes as "concert".

grammar.name: Ergative
grammar.description: AGENT or FORCE that causes the act

grammar.name: Inducive
grammar.explanation: The patient who undergoes the tangible effect, impact, or change of state of an act/event initiated/caused by that self-same party. Its semantic role is that of simultaneous AGENT and PATIENT.
grammar.guidance: IND marks the self-affected subject of the predicate (who acts and undergoes)—not manner or simile; prefer a subject NP (e.g. 'the boys run') over 'in the manner of X'

grammar.name: Possessive
grammar.explanation: A noun which has alienable (removable or severable) possession of another noun in the sense of having physical control or oversight of that noun, whether by chance circumstance or deliberate manipulation.
grammar.guidance: temporary/physical possession in use: prefer 'X's Y' for the item currently used/occupied (e.g. 'the rider's saddle [in use]')—not ownership-as-property

grammar.name: Proprietive
grammar.explanation: A noun having alienable possession of another noun in the sense of quasi-permanent contextual control, ownership or oversight, whether by societal recognition, social convention, law, purchase or decree.
grammar.guidance: proprietive ownership: prefer owned-property reading (e.g. 'the farmer's tractor')—contrast POS (in-use)

grammar.name: Genitive
grammar.explanation: A noun which has inalienable (unremovable, unseverable) possession of or association with another noun in the sense of having that noun as an inherent or intrinsic attribute, characteristic, physical part, or genetic (familial) bond.
grammar.guidance: intrinsic/whole-part genitive: prefer inalienable or constitutive 'of' (e.g. 'the lid of a jar' / 'the river's bank')

grammar.name: Attributive
grammar.explanation: A noun which inalienably experiences the effects of, or otherwise has an affective relationship with another noun, either as a temporary or permanent attribute, characteristic, or experience, whether physical or psychological, objective or subjective in nature.
grammar.guidance: attributive quality as possessed trait: prefer 'X's Y' for a quality/emotion (e.g. 'the singer's nervousness')

grammar.name: Productive
grammar.explanation: The creator, author or originator of another noun.
grammar.guidance: productive origin: prefer creator→product (e.g. 'the poet's essays')

grammar.name: Interpretive
grammar.description: subjective viewpoint through which X is interpreted
grammar.explanation: A noun acting as the subjective interpretational context of another noun, that is the noun by or through which another noun is subjectively interpreted or described.
grammar.guidance: interpretative viewpoint: prefer 'from X's point of view' / 'in X's reading' (e.g. 'from the judge's standpoint')

grammar.name: Originative
grammar.explanation: A noun as being the literal or figurative source of another, or which is the native location, origin, or usual locational context for another.
grammar.guidance: originative source: prefer 'fruit/product of X' origin (e.g. 'honey from the hive')

grammar.name: Interdependent
grammar.explanation: A noun which has a coordinated, tandem, complementary or mutually dependent relationship with another. The relationship between the two nouns can be thought of as reciprocal in nature.
grammar.guidance: interdependent part-whole: prefer constitutive containment (e.g. 'the marrow in the bone')

grammar.name: Partitive
grammar.explanation: A quantitative or content-to-container relationship between the two nouns. Also used to mark a noun qualified by a specific number.
grammar.guidance: partitive measure/group-of: prefer 'a load/batch of X' (e.g. 'a crate of bottles')

grammar.name: Applicative
grammar.description: circumstantial use or function of X
grammar.explanation: A noun which represents the purpose for which another noun is to be utilized in a given instance. Usually translates English 'for' when meaning 'for the temporary or incidental use/purpose of.'
grammar.guidance: With reciprocal social introduction, often synthesizes as purpose "to meet X".

grammar.name: Purposive
grammar.explanation: A noun which characterizes or defines the purpose of, or reason for, another noun. Defines another noun's dedicated function or primary reason for being, outside of any contextual instance.
grammar.guidance: purposive function-as-name: English often names the tool by purpose (e.g. 'a watering can')

grammar.name: Transmissive
grammar.explanation: A noun for whose sake or benefit an action or event occurs or is done or the party to whose detriment an action or event occurs.
grammar.guidance: transmissive beneficiary/recipient of transfer: prefer 'X for Y' as intended recipient (e.g. 'a letter for the neighbor')

grammar.name: Deferential
grammar.description: for X's sake / out of deference to X
grammar.explanation: Translates the English phrases 'out of respect for,' 'for the sake of,' or 'in deference toward,' identifying the noun to which deference is paid within the context for an act, condition, or event.
grammar.guidance: deferential motive: prefer 'out of respect for X' / 'in deference to X' (e.g. 'out of respect for custom')

grammar.name: Contrastive
grammar.description: instead of / in place of X
grammar.explanation: A noun which has been replaced by another or for which another noun has been substituted. Translatable by the English phrases 'instead of' or 'rather than' or 'as opposed to.'
grammar.guidance: contrastive not-that: prefer 'X, not Y' / 'rather than' (e.g. 'it's tea, not coffee')

grammar.name: Transpositive
grammar.explanation: Implies substitution of one noun for another. Translates English 'for' in the sense of 'on behalf of,' 'in place of,' or 'instead of' (i.e., 'as a substitution for').
grammar.guidance: transpositive substitution: prefer 'substituting X for Y' / 'replacing Y with X' (e.g. 'substituting ink for paint')

grammar.name: Commutative
grammar.explanation: Translates English 'for' in the sense of 'in exchange for.'
grammar.guidance: commutative exchange/payment framing: prefer 'paid/exchanged for X' (e.g. 'they paid for the lessons')

grammar.name: Comparative
grammar.explanation: A noun being compared to another. Translates such expressions as 'as compared to,' or certain usages of 'versus' or 'as opposed to.'
grammar.guidance: comparative standard: prefer 'X compared to Y' / 'X relative to Y' (e.g. 'bitter compared to honey')

grammar.name: Considerative
grammar.explanation: Translates English terms such as 'according to,' 'in the opinion of.'
grammar.guidance: considerative authority: prefer 'according to X' / 'in X's judgment' (e.g. 'according to the guide')

grammar.name: Functive
grammar.description: the manner in which X is/occurs
grammar.explanation: Functions similarly to English adverbs ending in -ly or the adverbial use of with, identifying the manner in which an action, event, or state occurs or exists.
grammar.guidance: functive manner: prefer manner adverb/PP of how the act is done (e.g. 'speaks confidently')

grammar.name: Transformative
grammar.description: into — the final state of a transformation
grammar.explanation: The outcome or final state of a process, often translatable by 'to,' 'until,' or 'into' in the sense of reaching a final state after having undergone some transformation.
grammar.guidance: transformative end-state as purpose of the act: prefer 'lessons/training into becoming X' reading—not mere payment-for

grammar.name: Classificative
grammar.explanation: A noun as a basis for arranging, sorting, classifying, or counting. Also identifies a noun considered in consecutively recurring increments as a means of describing the manner of an event.
grammar.guidance: classificative by class/unit: prefer 'X by X' / 'X-wise' / 'by the X' (e.g. 'page by page' / 'widthwise')

grammar.name: Resultative
grammar.explanation: A result or consequence, usually translatable utilizing a clause-like structure in English.
grammar.guidance: when chaining AVS/EML avoidance, prefer infinitive purpose 'to avoid being turned into X'—not 'resulting in avoiding…'

grammar.name: Consumptive
grammar.explanation: The resource consumed or used (up) as a result of, or as a concurrent part of a process.
grammar.guidance: consumptive means/ingredient: prefer 'with/using X as consumed means' (e.g. 'bakes bread with yeast')

grammar.name: Concessive
grammar.explanation: A noun, situation, or circumstance which gives rise to an expectation of a certain result which, in fact, does not occur.
grammar.guidance: concessive despite: prefer 'in spite of X' / 'despite X' (e.g. 'in spite of the delay')

grammar.name: Aversive
grammar.description: for fear of / in order to avoid
grammar.explanation: A noun as a source or object of fear and/or avoidance. Translates expressions such as 'for fear of,' 'in order to avoid,' or 'in avoidance of.'
grammar.guidance: aversive fear-motive: prefer 'out of fear of X' / 'for fear of X' (e.g. 'out of fear of silence')

grammar.name: Conversive
grammar.explanation: Used in conjunction with hypothetical or potential contexts to identify a hypothetical exception to a potential outcome or an actual circumstance which alters or has altered a potential outcome.
grammar.guidance: conversive exception: prefer 'except X' / 'all but X' (e.g. 'everything was packed except the lamp')

grammar.name: Situative
grammar.description: given / because of / in view of
grammar.explanation: A noun as the background context for a clause without implying a direct causative relationship between the background context and the act, condition, or event which occurs.
grammar.guidance: situative because-of-presence: cause is X's presence/existence, not an act by X (e.g. 'upset because of the crowd [being there]')

grammar.name: Pertinential
grammar.explanation: A formative functioning as the general referent of the verb, translating such English terms as 'about,' 'regarding,' 'concerning,' 'in regard to,' 'in reference to,' 'pertaining to,' or 'as for.'
grammar.guidance: Marks the about-topic; other quoted stems in the same formative may be distinct participants.

grammar.name: Descriptive
grammar.explanation: A formative as describing another formative in an adjectival manner, translatable as 'characterised/describable as being like', 'characterized/describable as having the quality/qualities of'.
grammar.guidance: descriptive case-frame: relative/descriptive clause characterizing the head (e.g. 'bird-watching hikers tend to wake early')—do not promote the frame to a main-clause only reading

grammar.name: Correlative
grammar.description: in relation to / in association with
grammar.explanation: An abstract general relationship, association, or conjunction between one formative and another, including subjective, contextual, metaphorical, or symbolic associations.
grammar.guidance: correlative association/theme: prefer 'in the direction of X' or 'X in Y' thematic link (e.g. 'symbols in folklore')

grammar.name: Compositive
grammar.explanation: A formative as being the literal or figurative substance or component(s) of which another is made, composed, formed, built or comprised.
grammar.guidance: compositive material: prefer 'made of X' / 'of X' (e.g. 'things made of glass')

grammar.name: Comitative
grammar.explanation: A formative that accompanies another, translatable as '(along) with'.
grammar.guidance: comitative accompaniment (not worn): prefer 'with X' as accompanying object carried along (e.g. 'a traveler with a suitcase')—contrast UTL

grammar.name: Utilitative
grammar.explanation: A formative in the process of being used while some other activity or state is in progress.
grammar.guidance: utilitative worn/in-use tool: prefer 'wearing/using X' (e.g. 'a traveler wearing a coat')—contrast COM

grammar.name: Predicative
grammar.explanation: The non-causal basis, foundation, sustenance (literally or figuratively), or required existential condition for another noun or clause, translatable by the phrases 'based (up)on,' 'dependent (up)on' or 'relying on.'
grammar.guidance: predicative basis: prefer 'based in/on X' (e.g. 'rules based in evidence')

grammar.name: Activative
grammar.description: experiencer of a modal state (want, need, ability)
grammar.explanation: Identifies the experiencer of a modal state, such as obligation, necessity, desire, hope, expectation, wishing, being able to, etc. functioning as the "subject" of a modal(ized) verb governing a hypothetical state (i.e., what is wanted, needed, expected, able to be done, etc.).
grammar.guidance: activative enablement/activation: often a modal 'even X needs Y' / enabling frame (e.g. 'I think even machines need care')—do not drop the validating matrix if present

grammar.name: Assimilative
grammar.description: as if it were X (analogy / metaphor)
grammar.explanation: Identifies a formative used as a context for analogy or metaphorical comparison, translatable as 'as/like' meaning 'as if it were X'
grammar.guidance: assimilative likeness without identity: prefer 'like an X (though not one)' (e.g. 'you argue like a lawyer [though you are not]')

grammar.name: Essive
grammar.explanation: Identifies the role or name by which an entity is known or contextually identified, translates 'as/like' in sense of naming or functional identity
grammar.guidance: essive identity-as: prefer 'like an X (because you are one)' / 'as an X' (e.g. 'you argue like a lawyer [being one]')

grammar.name: Terminative
grammar.description: goal of an act — toward / for
grammar.explanation: Identifies a formative as being the goal of an act/event
grammar.guidance: terminative goal of seeking: prefer bare goal NP of pursuit (e.g. 'we're seeking mushrooms')

grammar.name: Selective
grammar.description: every X / on Xs (recurring entity or period)
grammar.explanation: Identifies a contextually recurring time-period or string of recurring entities
grammar.guidance: selective every-nth / subset pick: prefer 'every nth X' / 'each selected X' (e.g. 'every fourth row')

grammar.name: Conformative
grammar.description: pursuant to / in conformance with X
grammar.explanation: Identifies the entity pursuant to which, as per which, or in conformance with which another entity is or an act/event occurs
grammar.guidance: On a prior formative, English "Under / pursuant to X" frames the following modal act; do not make X the direct object of the verb in the next formative unless the gloss marks object case on X.

grammar.name: Dependent
grammar.explanation: Identifies a formative as being the basis of a dependency phrase on which another formative acts as contingency
grammar.guidance: dependent conditional circumstance: prefer 'only if X' / 'provided X' (e.g. 'will attend only if there is music')

grammar.name: Locative
grammar.explanation: Identifies the location where something is situated or occurs, translates 'at/in/on/by'
grammar.guidance: locative at/in place: prefer 'at/in X' static location (e.g. 'at the gate')

grammar.name: Attendant
grammar.description: in the presence of X (witness, peripheral party)

grammar.name: Allative
grammar.explanation: Identifies the entity toward which another entity is moving/approaching, translates 'to/toward'
grammar.guidance: allative toward goal: prefer 'to(ward) X' (e.g. 'toward the harbor')

grammar.name: Ablative
grammar.explanation: Identifies the entity away from which another entity is moving/receding, translates '(away) from'
grammar.guidance: ablative away-from source: prefer 'away from X' / 'from X' (e.g. 'walk away from the platform')

grammar.name: Orientative
grammar.explanation: Identifies the entity (often a body part or sub-component) which serves as the "face" or surface or "front" or "head" of an entity in terms of external communication or interaction, or which serves as the forward "end" of a spatially orientated axis aligned to a vector of motion in terms of directional movement
grammar.guidance: with motion verbs + body-part/orientation stems (front, back, flank/side), prefer directional adverbs (frontward, backward, sideways)—not path PPs (along the side / toward the back)

grammar.name: Interrelative
grammar.description: relative to X (directional or temporal position)
grammar.explanation: Identifies the directional/temporal orientation or position of an entity relative to another
grammar.guidance: interrelative temporal relation focus: keep the between-times relation (e.g. 'how long since the train's arrival?' as relation-between-times)—not mere clock time

grammar.name: Intrative
grammar.description: since / until / from X (boundary of a span)
grammar.explanation: Identifies a formative as being the spatio-temporal boundary point of a span or volume of space or period of time
grammar.guidance: intrative juxtaposition of two times/events: focus on the span between endpoints (e.g. 'how long between departure and return')

grammar.name: Navigative
grammar.explanation: Identifies the entity whose literal or metaphorically inferred long axis serves as the direction of another entity's path or trajectory
grammar.guidance: navigative path/way followed: prefer 'follow the way/path of X' (e.g. 'they follow the river's course')

grammar.name: Concursive
grammar.description: at or during the time of X (temporal locative)

grammar.name: Assessive
grammar.explanation: Identifies the increment of space or time or unit by which a contextual ratio of measurement is created
grammar.guidance: assessive rate/ratio: prefer 'X per Y' / 'X for each Y'

grammar.name: Periodic
grammar.description: within / over X (time span for repetitions)
grammar.explanation: Identifies the span of time/time frame at some point(s) during which separate events, repetitions, or durationally segmented acts or states take place
grammar.guidance: time frame for a (segmented) act's completion: prefer "it takes X" / "in X" / "within X"—do not render as a past-event setting adjunct "over an X period"; contrast PRO ("for an hour" = how long an act lasts)

grammar.name: Prolapsive
grammar.explanation: Identifies the duration of an act, condition, or event, i.e. how long it takes or lasts
grammar.guidance: how long an act lasts: prefer "for X" / "through X" / "all X"—contrast PER ("it takes X" / "in/within X" for time-to-completion)

grammar.name: Postcursive
grammar.explanation: Identifies an entity acting as a point in time after which an act, state, or event occurs
grammar.guidance: point-in-time after which: keep "after …" / "it was after …"; with RTR+CRL (outburst) formative, prefer PCR as a past-event frame over a bare ongoing "there's a … going on"; when FRAMED attend/event precedes, keep attendees + attend verb

grammar.name: Static
grammar.description: entity as a state, condition, or quality

grammar.name: Dynamic
grammar.description: entity as a dynamic event or action

grammar.name: Basic
grammar.description: holistic instantiation, prior to other specifications

grammar.name: Objective
grammar.description: tangible tool/object/patient associated with the act/state

grammar.name: Existential
grammar.explanation: ontologically objective features that exist irrespective of observers, opinions, or interpretations
grammar.guidance: existential context: render as a bare physical scene (e.g. 'rain falls on the roof') with no social/metaphorical overlay

grammar.name: Functional
grammar.explanation: features defined socially by ideas, attitudes, beliefs, opinions, convention, cultural status, use, function, benefit
grammar.guidance: functional context: highlight personal/social significance of the scene (e.g. 'the letter arriving mattered for the family')

grammar.name: Representational
grammar.explanation: symbol, metaphor, or metonym, representing some other concept or entity abstractly associated with it
grammar.guidance: representational context: treat participants as metaphorical/stand-ins (e.g. 'the storm stood for the argument')

grammar.name: Amalgamative
grammar.explanation: systemic, holistic, gestalt-like nature derived from interrelationships between all parts and developmental history
grammar.guidance: amalgamative context: blend emotional impact with cultural meaning (e.g. 'the ceremony hit hard and carried tradition')

grammar.name: Duplex
grammar.explanation: binary or two-halved in nature — a configurational set of exactly two entities, events, or states viewed as a paired or bipartite whole
grammar.guidance: duplex pair: prefer 'a pair of X' / 'two X as a unit' (e.g. 'a pair of boots')—not bare plural

grammar.name: Duplex Similar Separate
grammar.explanation: Two entities, similar and physically separate
grammar.guidance: duplex similar separate: two alike items as a pair but not joined (e.g. 'a pair of matching cups kept apart')

grammar.name: Duplex Similar Connected
grammar.explanation: Two entities, similar and connected
grammar.guidance: duplex similar connected: two alike items linked as a pair (e.g. 'a pair of linked rings')

grammar.name: Duplex Similar Fused
grammar.explanation: Two entities, similar and fused
grammar.guidance: duplex similar fused: two alike items fused into one pair-unit (e.g. 'a fused pair of identical plates')

grammar.name: Duplex Dissimilar Separate
grammar.explanation: Two entities, dissimilar and physically separate
grammar.guidance: duplex dissimilar separate: two unlike items as a loose pair (e.g. 'a mismatched pair of gloves')

grammar.name: Duplex Fuzzy Separate
grammar.description: two instances of indeterminate similarity, separate

grammar.name: Duplex Fuzzy Connected
grammar.description: two instances of indeterminate similarity, connected

grammar.name: Duplex Fuzzy Fused
grammar.description: two instances of indeterminate similarity, fused

grammar.name: Multiplex Similar Separate
grammar.description: three or more similar instances, separate
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, similar and physically separate — a multiplex set whose members are alike but not physically connected
grammar.guidance: multiplex similar separate: many alike items, unjoined (e.g. 'a loose set of matching tiles')

grammar.name: Multiplex Similar Connected
grammar.description: three or more similar instances, connected
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, similar and connected — a multiplex set whose members are alike and physically touching or linked
grammar.guidance: multiplex similar connected: many alike items touching/linked (e.g. 'a chain of identical beads')

grammar.name: Multiplex Similar Fused
grammar.description: three or more similar instances, fused
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, similar and fused
grammar.guidance: multiplex similar fused: many alike items fused (e.g. 'a fused cluster of identical crystals')

grammar.name: Multiplex Dissimilar Separate
grammar.description: three or more dissimilar instances, separate
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, dissimilar and physically separate — a multiplex set whose members differ from one another and are not physically connected
grammar.guidance: multiplex dissimilar separate: many unlike items, unjoined (e.g. 'a mixed pile of tools')

grammar.name: Multiplex Dissimilar Connected
grammar.description: three or more dissimilar instances, connected
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, dissimilar and connected — a multiplex set whose members differ from one another but are physically touching or linked
grammar.guidance: multiplex dissimilar connected: many unlike items linked/touching (e.g. 'linked odd-sized modules')

grammar.name: Multiplex Dissimilar Fused
grammar.description: three or more dissimilar instances, fused
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, dissimilar and fused
grammar.guidance: multiplex dissimilar fused: many unlike items fused (e.g. 'a fused mass of mixed scrap')

grammar.name: Multiplex Fuzzy Separate
grammar.description: three or more instances of indeterminate similarity, separate
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, fuzzy in similarity and physically separate
grammar.guidance: multiplex fuzzy separate: loosely similar-looking items, unjoined (e.g. 'assorted vaguely round pebbles, some more than others')

grammar.name: Multiplex Fuzzy Connected
grammar.description: three or more instances of indeterminate similarity, connected
grammar.explanation: Three or more entities, fuzzy in similarity and connected
grammar.guidance: multiplex fuzzy connected: loosely similar-looking items linked (e.g. 'linked vaguely rounded beads, some more than others')

grammar.name: Multiplex Fuzzy Fused
grammar.description: three or more instances of indeterminate similarity, fused

grammar.name: Coalescent
grammar.description: members combine into a single function

grammar.name: Nomic
grammar.explanation: generic collective entity or archetype, containing all members or instantiations of a configurative set throughout space and time
grammar.guidance: nomic generic: with 'child'-N or creature/person stems prefer plural generic subjects (e.g. 'children'); with habit/verb stems prefer generic/habitual practice—not a one-off deictic instance and do not invent a bare 'they' subject from N alone

grammar.name: Proximal
grammar.explanation: indicates that a noun is being spoken of not in its entirety, but rather only in terms of the portion, duration, subset, or aspect which is relevant to the context at hand
grammar.guidance: when PRX marks the main eventive formative with no case-marked actor, prefer impersonal 'takes place' / 'going on' over calquing 'stretch/portion of'; when PRX marks a noun, keep natural existential English (e.g. 'if there's an X')

grammar.name: Normal
grammar.description: the entity as it actually exists
grammar.explanation: Real-world actualities — the formative denotes entities, acts, or states taken as actually existing in the real world rather than imagined or representative counterparts
grammar.guidance: normal/real-world framing: prefer a plain factual clause (e.g. 'the guard notices a shadow')—not hypothetical/representative wording

grammar.name: Representative
grammar.explanation: Alternative/imagined counterparts — the formative denotes entities, acts, or states as imagined, hypothetical, or representative rather than as real-world actualities
grammar.guidance: hypothetical/representative—not always agent "imagine"; with Nomic participants (generic person/creature stems), prefer infinitival/generic framing (e.g. "for an X to VERB a Y")—do not add "imagine having…"

grammar.name: Monoactive
grammar.explanation: The default valence indicating a lack of co-activity, no participation by a second party is implied
grammar.guidance: monoactive: no co-activity implied; parties may share a scene without interacting (e.g. 'two bakers work in the kitchen [each on their own]')

grammar.name: Parallel
grammar.description: two or more parallel co-actors doing the same action
grammar.explanation: Indicates that a second party is engaging in the same activity as the first party at same time
grammar.guidance: parallel: same kind of activity at the same time, separately (e.g. 'two bakers knead dough at the same time, separately')

grammar.name: Corollary
grammar.description: one party's action is a corollary of another's
grammar.explanation: Similar to parallel, except that the second party engages in related activity at the same time as the first party
grammar.guidance: corollary: simultaneous related but different activities (e.g. 'two bakers work at once, each on a different recipe')

grammar.name: Reciprocal
grammar.explanation: Indicates identical activity by one party directed at another party and vice-versa. English may be 'each other'/'one another' when the reciprocal partners are a named closed set (often SBS-marked), or reciprocity with an unnamed external party when only a single group party is named without SBS.
grammar.guidance: If two or more parties are separately named (distinct formatives/stems), render reciprocity among those named parties. If a single plural/group/duplex party is named without SBS, do not say 'each other'—imply an unnamed external reciprocal partner (e.g. 'playing with another party', not 'with each other'). SBS1-1 on that group marks closed-set 'each other' within the group. A separate PRN formative is the about-topic. Pattern: DPX group-IND + RCP without SBS → reciprocity with an unnamed external party; same gloss + SBS1-1 → closed-set 'with each other'.

grammar.name: Complementary
grammar.description: complementary actions, each completing the other
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the second party performs a complementary activity to that of the first party, the "other half" of the joint activity
grammar.guidance: complementary: interlocking roles of one joint activity (e.g. 'two bakers run a complementary bake—one mixes, one shapes')

grammar.name: Duplicative
grammar.description: duplicative — same action repeated in parallel
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the second party copies or repeats the activity of the first party
grammar.guidance: duplicative: one party does the act and the other copies it (e.g. 'one baker demonstrates kneading and the other copies')

grammar.name: Demonstrative
grammar.description: demonstrative — one party shows another how
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the first party demonstrates for the second party how to do something or what to do
grammar.guidance: demonstrative: one shows the other how (e.g. 'one baker shows the other how to score the loaf')

grammar.name: Contingent
grammar.description: contingent — one action depends on another
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the second party engages in the next or dependent phase of a multi-part activity
grammar.guidance: Sequential/dependent phases of one multi-part activity: one party completes one part, then the other does the next logical part. Do not collapse to 'together'/'with each other' (RCP±SBS), simultaneous complementary roles (CPL), or copying the same act (DUP). Prefer explicit sequencing ('one … then the other … the next part'). E.g. starting a campfire for a friend in CNG implies the friend then cooks.

grammar.name: Participative
grammar.description: participative — taking part in a wider group action
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the parties take part in an activity involving a greater whole, translatable by 'take part in'
grammar.guidance: participative: both take part in the same shared activity (e.g. 'two bakers take part in the same bake')

grammar.name: Punctual
grammar.explanation: Describes an act, condition, or event which is point-like, momentary or instantaneous in nature, such as an explosion, a flash of lightning, a single handclap, or a single cough. It can be visually represented along a timeline by a single point.
grammar.guidance: punctual: single brief occurrence (e.g. 'the bell gave one short ring')

grammar.name: Iterative
grammar.explanation: Refers to a momentary event which repeats itself in a rapid, on/off, staccato manner, considered as a single event
grammar.guidance: iterative: a series of short occurrences (e.g. 'the bell gave a series of short rings')

grammar.name: Repetitive
grammar.explanation: Refers to a relatively brief event repeated in an on/off staccato manner
grammar.guidance: repetitive: a series of longer occurrences (e.g. 'the bell gave a series of long rings')

grammar.name: Intermittent
grammar.explanation: Similar to iterative but the duration of time between repetitions is relatively long and contextually relevant
grammar.guidance: intermittent: a repeating short occurrence pattern (e.g. 'the bell kept giving a repeating short ring')

grammar.name: Recurrent
grammar.explanation: Indicates a slow repetition of an event, where the duration between occurrences is relatively long
grammar.guidance: slow recurrence; with bouncing/jumping verbs, English often uses '(up and down)' rather than the literal phrase 'slowly recurring'

grammar.name: Frequentative
grammar.explanation: Indicates an iterative occurrence which in turn repeats at intervals, the whole considered as a single event
grammar.guidance: frequentative: repeating series of singles (e.g. 'the bell gave repeating series of single rings')

grammar.name: Fragmentative
grammar.explanation: Indicates a random pattern of punctual occurrences, the whole considered as a single event
grammar.guidance: fragmentative: several random series of repeating shorts (e.g. 'several random bursts of repeating short rings')

grammar.name: Vacillative
grammar.explanation: Functions as a non-punctual counterpart to the fragmentative
grammar.guidance: vacillitative: several random series of repeating longs (e.g. 'several random bursts of repeating long rings')

grammar.name: Fluctuative
grammar.explanation: Indicates a random pattern of both punctual and longer occurrences
grammar.guidance: random punctual bursts / snippets; with sing.a.song+RSM+PRL, prefer fragmented/burst song snippets—not bare 'intermittently'

grammar.name: Beneficial to speaker
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is of benefit to the first-person speaker of the sentence
grammar.guidance: when bundled as PA+1M/BEN (or similar multiparty+speaker), benefit scopes over the whole party ("to our benefit" / we)—not speaker-alone "to my benefit"

grammar.name: Beneficial to addressee
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is of benefit to the addressee of the sentence
grammar.guidance: beneficial to addressee: benefit scopes to 'you'/'your side' (e.g. weather/news framed as good for the hearer)

grammar.name: Beneficial to 3rd party
grammar.description: beneficial to an unspecified third party
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is of benefit to a third party other than the speaker or addressee
grammar.guidance: beneficial to a third party: benefit scopes to that third party (e.g. 'the patient's recovery has returned' as good for them)

grammar.name: Beneficial to self
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is of benefit to the formative itself to which the affix is attached
grammar.guidance: beneficial to self: self-benefactive announcement/state (e.g. present a favorable outcome for the speaker without a separate 'I declare' matrix)

grammar.name: Unknown
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is either of unknown benefit or detriment or that any benefit/detriment is irrelevant
grammar.guidance: unknown benefit/detriment: keep evaluative neutrality (e.g. 'there's an odd object in the field' with no good/bad spin)

grammar.name: Detrimental to self
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is detrimental to the formative itself to which the affix is attached
grammar.guidance: detrimental to self: self-directed negative evaluation (e.g. self-reproach force without inventing extra parties)

grammar.name: Detrimental to 3rd party
grammar.description: detrimental to an unspecified third party
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is detrimental to a third party other than the speaker or addressee
grammar.guidance: detrimental to a third party: harm/ill scopes to that party (e.g. 'the neighbor's debt has returned')

grammar.name: Detrimental to addressee
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is detrimental to the addressee of the sentence
grammar.guidance: detrimental to addressee: bad-for-you scoping (e.g. reported news framed as disadvantageous to the hearer)

grammar.name: Detrimental to speaker
grammar.explanation: Indicates that the formative is detrimental to the first-person speaker of the sentence
grammar.guidance: detrimental to speaker: bad-for-me scoping on the focused content (e.g. identifying a situation as undesirable for the speaker)

grammar.name: Equative
grammar.explanation: X M 's the same as Y ( or as before) / X is as M as Y ( or as before)
grammar.guidance: equative level: prefer 'as … as' equality between compared parties

grammar.name: Surpassive
grammar.explanation: X M 's more than Y ( or than before) / X is more M than Y ( or than before)
grammar.guidance: surpassive relative greater degree: prefer comparative 'longer/more than' with optional neither-extreme caveat—keep relative, not absolute

grammar.name: Precessive
grammar.explanation: Conveys that an action, state or event has immediately preceded
grammar.guidance: precessive recent past: prefer 'just (now) …' (e.g. 'I just noticed a stranger at the gate')

grammar.name: Regulative
grammar.explanation: Conveys the idea of participation or involvement in an action, state, or event over an amount of time extending from the past into the future relative to the contextual present
grammar.guidance: regulative habitual ongoing: prefer 'have been …-ing (everywhere/habitually)' (e.g. 'couriers have been busy delivering parcels everywhere')

grammar.name: Summative
grammar.explanation: Translates English '...(have) already...'
grammar.guidance: summative already-complete: prefer 'have already finished X' (e.g. 'they have already finished packing')

grammar.name: Cessative
grammar.explanation: Conveys the idea of cessation of an event, state or action
grammar.guidance: cessative stop: prefer 'stopped/ceased X-ing' (e.g. 'they stopped packing')

grammar.name: Pausal
grammar.explanation: Indicates a pause in an action, state or event, with an implied intention to resume
grammar.guidance: pausal pause-in: prefer 'paused in X-ing' (e.g. 'they paused in packing')

grammar.name: Regressive
grammar.explanation: Conveys the idea of a return to an original or previous action, state or event after a long hiatus involving an intervening change of state or situation
grammar.guidance: regressive return-to: prefer 'got back to X' after interruption (e.g. 'after the break, she got back to studying')

grammar.name: Preclusive
grammar.explanation: Conveys the fact that an action, state, or event takes place from inception to conclusion all in one contextual segment
grammar.guidance: preclusive all-at-once/whole: prefer 'X whole' / undivided completion (e.g. 'swallowed the pill whole')

grammar.name: Incessative
grammar.explanation: Conveys that an action, state or event continues on without stopping
grammar.guidance: incessative keeps-on: prefer 'keeps X-ing on and on' (e.g. 'keeps rambling on and on')

grammar.name: Experiential
grammar.explanation: Translates English 'ever' in the sense of 'within the realm of one's experience'
grammar.guidance: experiential ever-in-life: prefer 'Have you ever …?' (e.g. 'Have you ever seen a comet?')

grammar.name: Interruptive
grammar.explanation: Translates English 'to get interrupted while X-ing' or 'to X only so far or so much before having to stop'
grammar.guidance: interruptive broken-by: prefer 'was interrupted by X' (e.g. 'the meeting was interrupted by an alarm')

grammar.name: Preemptive
grammar.explanation: Emphasizes the singularity and initial occurrence an action, state or event
grammar.guidance: preemptive first-time/at-last milestone: prefer 'finally/for the first time' milestone reading (e.g. 'the apprentice finally soloed')—not mere delay

grammar.name: Climactic
grammar.explanation: Emphasizes the finality of an action, state or event
grammar.guidance: climactic last-straw: prefer 'for the last time' culminating warning (e.g. 'you've lied for the last time')

grammar.name: Dilatory
grammar.explanation: Translates English '(be) long-delay(ed) in being/doing X'
grammar.guidance: long delay: with CPT-'seek'+AFM, keep both long-delay and certainty—do not collapse to bare 'finally'

grammar.name: Temporary
grammar.explanation: Conveys that an action, state or event is being considered or is applicable only to the present subjective context
grammar.guidance: temporary present-context only: prefer "for the time being" / "for now"—do not drop the temporary sense

grammar.name: Expenditive
grammar.explanation: Conveys an all-consuming action, state, or event which interferes with or prevents other events from occurring
grammar.guidance: expenditive wasteful spending of time/resource: prefer 'wastes time/resources X-ing' (e.g. 'wastes hours on idle speculation')

grammar.name: Limitative
grammar.explanation: Translates English 'to be/do X (just) in time' indicating an act/event that culminates an anticipatory context
grammar.guidance: limitative just-in-time boundary: prefer 'just in time to …' (e.g. 'left just in time to avoid the storm')

grammar.name: Expeditive
grammar.explanation: Conveys a sense of haste associated with an action or event
grammar.guidance: expeditive hurried manner: prefer 'in a hurry' / 'hastily' (e.g. 'they packed in a hurry')

grammar.name: Protractive
grammar.explanation: Conveys that an action, state or event takes place over a long period of time
grammar.guidance: protractive long-ongoing: prefer 'for quite a while' / extended duration so far (e.g. 'it's been snowing for quite a while')

grammar.name: Preparatory
grammar.explanation: Conveys that an action, state or event exists or takes place in advance of another
grammar.guidance: preparatory in-advance: prefer 'planned/prepared X in advance' (e.g. 'they planned the route in advance')

grammar.name: Disclusive
grammar.explanation: Focuses on the revelatory nature of an action, state or event
grammar.guidance: revelatory frame: prefer "it turns out …" / "as it turns out"—do not omit the revelatory matrix

grammar.name: Conclusive
grammar.explanation: Conveys the direct outcome of an action, state or event within the short-term context of the situation at hand
grammar.guidance: conclusive ended-up result: prefer 'we've ended up …' / final landing (e.g. 'we've ended up in the old district')

grammar.name: Culminative
grammar.explanation: Similar to the conclusive above, but with a focus on the eventual, long-term outcome over an extended period of time
grammar.guidance: culminative eventual outcome: prefer 'eventually wound up …' (e.g. 'we eventually wound up in the old district')—contrast CCL's more final 'ended up'

grammar.name: Tardative
grammar.explanation: Conveys the idea that an action, state, or event lessens, dwindles, or slackens in energy, intensity, or effect
grammar.guidance: tardative gradual waning: prefer progressive decline over time (e.g. 'enthusiasm wanes as the years go by')

grammar.name: Transitional
grammar.explanation: Focuses on the initial stage of preparation, adjustment, or accustomization to an action, state or event
grammar.guidance: transitional taking-up new state: prefer 'has taken up X as …' (e.g. 'has taken up painting as a pastime')

grammar.name: Intercommutative
grammar.explanation: Conveys the idea of "sequential reciprocity," meaning that the action or event is a consequent reciprocation triggered by, or in reaction to, an initiating action or event
grammar.guidance: intercommutative mutual return-act: prefer reciprocal 'X back' (e.g. 'couldn't help but glance back with curiosity')

grammar.name: Motive
grammar.explanation: Conveys that an action, state or event involves physical removal or absence of the participant from the present context of discourse
grammar.guidance: motive let's-head-off: prefer hortative motion 'let's head off to X' (e.g. 'let's head off to the coast')

grammar.name: Sequential
grammar.explanation: conveys the idea a "sequential progressive" in which a series of contextually identical instances is seen as comprising a single event
grammar.guidance: sequential one-by-one: prefer 'one by one' / itemized sequence (e.g. 'checked each box one by one')

grammar.name: Natural case-scope
grammar.description: default — case follows clause head or main verb

grammar.name: Antecedent case-scope
grammar.description: head — governs case of clause's unmarked nouns

grammar.name: Directive
grammar.explanation: the statement is either an imperative command to another party to do/be something, or a "commissive" statement committing the speaker to a specific state or course of action
grammar.guidance: directive command: prefer imperative to the addressee (e.g. 'Walk away from the platform!')

grammar.name: Declarative
grammar.explanation: a "performative" statement which. by its utterance/publication, creates a change of state (at least psychologically) for the addressees
grammar.guidance: do not add a matrix 'I hereby declare that…' clause; prefer direct announcement/presentation force (e.g. 'Here's…' / 'We have…' / 'What a…!'); with compete.to.win+ACCESSOR-IND+SLF:BEN, announce the winner in 2nd/3rd-person presentation force—never 1st-person 'I declare myself the winner' / 'I've won'

grammar.name: Interrogative
grammar.explanation: a statement whose purpose is to inquire or seek information from the addressee
grammar.guidance: interrogative content question: keep wh-question force on the queried relation/time/place

grammar.name: Verificative
grammar.explanation: a statement whose purpose is to seek/obtain corroboration, confirmation, or verification
grammar.guidance: verificative yes/no check: prefer a polar question seeking confirmation (e.g. 'Are the guests ready?')

grammar.name: Admonitive
grammar.explanation: a statement whose purpose is to provide advisory/admonitive information to the addressee
grammar.guidance: admonitive warning: prefer 'Beware of …!' / warning imperative (e.g. 'Beware of thin ice!')

grammar.name: Potentiative
grammar.explanation: a statement of wishing, hoping, or other unreal(ized) provenance
grammar.guidance: when OBG (must/have to) + ACT co-occur, prefer obligation ("must") over stacking "hope" from POT

grammar.name: Hortative
grammar.explanation: a counterfactual statement indicating a desired but impossible state of affairs that cannot be realized
grammar.guidance: counterfactual wish: "If only …"; with NEG on pathogen stem + ADI illness, the wish is that the ABS party GET the disease—not that they remain not-ill

grammar.name: Conjectural
grammar.explanation: Equivalent to an English-language "if"-clause, indicating that the statement is offered as a conjectured hypothetical
grammar.guidance: conjectural if-then speculation: prefer 'If you …, there'll be …' conjectural consequence (e.g. 'If you enter the cave, there'll be no easy return')

grammar.name: Observational
grammar.description: present sensory knowledge — I perceive / I know
grammar.explanation: present sensory knowledge or present sensory experience
grammar.guidance: epistemic source; do not add a separate "I perceive that…" matrix clause when the clause already has an explicit case-marked subject; on impersonal/eventive clauses with no case-marked actor, prefer 'takes place' / 'there's … going on' — do not add 'is observed'

grammar.name: Recollective
grammar.explanation: past sensory knowledge or past sensory experience — the speaker's knowledge derives from prior direct perception or memory rather than present observation
grammar.guidance: recollective remembered knowledge: keep as recalled fact (e.g. 'A lived longer than B…' as remembered), not newly inferred

grammar.name: Purportive
grammar.description: from a verifiable source — I've read / an expert says
grammar.explanation: knowledge from a definitive/(quasi-)verifiable 3rd party source
grammar.guidance: purportive alleged/yet-to: prefer 'had not yet …' / purported timeline claim (e.g. 'cities had not yet formed in that era')

grammar.name: Reportive
grammar.explanation: knowledge from a 3rd party
grammar.guidance: reportive hearsay: prefer a hearsay matrix ('I'm told…' / 'I hear…') before the reported clause

grammar.name: Unspecified
grammar.explanation: Validation deliberately unspecified — the speaker makes no commitment as to the epistemic source or evidentiary basis for the statement
grammar.guidance: unspecified validation: no special evidential matrix—render the clause plainly (e.g. a plain milestone statement)

grammar.name: Imaginary
grammar.explanation: unreal statement, not intended as true, based on whim, imagination, dream, altered mental state, etc.
grammar.guidance: imaginary validation: treat as imagined/unreal (e.g. 'there's a dragon in the attic' as imaginary)

grammar.name: Conventional
grammar.description: shared cultural knowledge — they say / it is said
grammar.explanation: cultural/conventional (i.e., collectively agreed-upon) knowledge
grammar.guidance: often surfaces as "They say…" / "It is said…"

grammar.name: Intuitive
grammar.description: intuition / hunch — I feel / something tells me
grammar.explanation: intuition, hunch, subjective feeling, past experiences, etc.
grammar.guidance: When ITU validates a modal/nomic formative with ACT (no separate speaker formative), render speaker intuition with a matrix like 'I think…' (do not omit it). When a case-marked subject already carries perceptual content (OBS/see patterns), omit redundant matrix 'I think/feel'.

grammar.name: Inferential
grammar.description: inferred from evidence — I infer / I reason
grammar.explanation: inference from evidence (or absence of alternatives), induction, extrapolation, etc.
grammar.guidance: inferential must-be: prefer 'must be …' inference (e.g. 'the guests must be ready')

grammar.name: Dismissive
grammar.description: is that it? / big deal / so what?

grammar.name: Pessimistic
grammar.description: yeah, like it really matters / pfft

grammar.name: Dubitative
grammar.description: hmm, not likely / I doubt it

grammar.name: Skeptical
grammar.description: yeah, right! / like anyone'd believe that!

grammar.name: Trepidative
grammar.description: oh God / oh no / oh dear (fear)

grammar.name: Apprehensive
grammar.description: I'm worried / I've got a bad feeling

grammar.name: Anticipative
grammar.explanation: Form: lst. 'I'm looking foward to this!'
grammar.guidance: anticipative bias: speaker anticipation/expectation color (e.g. anticipatory 'I…' / awaiting tone)—do not invent extra propositions

grammar.name: Indignative
grammar.explanation: Form: pšç. 'The nerve!' or 'How dare…!?"
grammar.guidance: indignative bias: offense/affront (e.g. 'The nerve!')

grammar.name: Repulsive
grammar.explanation: Form: šš. 'Yuck! Ew! How gross!'
grammar.guidance: repulsive bias: disgust (e.g. 'Yuck! How gross!')

grammar.name: Invidious
grammar.description: why does X get to and I don't?! / how unfair!

grammar.name: Perplexive
grammar.description: huh?! / WTF? / you gotta be kidding!

grammar.name: Disconcertive
grammar.description: I'm not sure about this / out of my element

grammar.name: Revelative
grammar.description: no wonder! / so that's why! / a-ha!

grammar.name: Euphoric
grammar.explanation: Form: gzz. '(Sigh) What bliss!'
grammar.guidance: euphoric bias: blissful affect (e.g. '(Sigh) What bliss!')

grammar.name: Delectative
grammar.explanation: Form: ẓm. 'Whee!'
grammar.guidance: delectative bias: playful delight (e.g. 'Whee!' / gleeful tone)

grammar.name: Solicitative
grammar.explanation: Form: ňň. 'please'
grammar.guidance: solicitative bias: please/request softener (e.g. 'please')

grammar.name: Mandatory
grammar.description: take it or leave it / this is your last chance

grammar.name: Exigent
grammar.explanation: Form: rrs. 'It's now or never!'
grammar.guidance: exigent bias: urgent/pressing tone on the clause (e.g. clipped urgency)—do not invent a new main verb

grammar.name: Attentive
grammar.description: well, whaddya know / look at that

grammar.name: Contensive
grammar.description: I told you so / you see?!

grammar.name: Accidental
grammar.description: as luck would have it / what luck!

grammar.name: Archetypal
grammar.description: what a...! / boy, did X ever...!

grammar.name: Presumptive
grammar.description: it can only mean one thing / and that's that!

grammar.name: Corrective
grammar.description: that is to say... / what I mean is...

grammar.name: Euphemistic
grammar.description: let's just say... / let me put it this way...

grammar.name: Propositive
grammar.description: what if... / consider this / posit that...

grammar.name: Suggestive
grammar.description: how about... / we could... / might I suggest...

grammar.name: Reflective
grammar.description: as I see it / in my opinion

grammar.name: Desperative
grammar.description: I'm afraid... / I don't know how to say this

grammar.name: Coincidental
grammar.explanation: Form: šš. 'What a coincidence!'
grammar.guidance: coincidental bias: prefer coincidence framing (e.g. 'What a coincidence!')

grammar.name: Fortuitous
grammar.description: it's just as well / all's well that ends well

grammar.name: Annunciative
grammar.description: guess what! / wait till you hear this!

grammar.name: Implicative
grammar.description: of course / after all / needless to say

grammar.name: Dejective
grammar.explanation: Form: žž. '(sigh)' [of dejection/disillusionment]
grammar.guidance: dejective bias: weary/sigh affect (e.g. a parenthetical sigh)—do not add propositional content

grammar.name: Discursive
grammar.explanation: Indicates a phrase/statement represents direct speech
grammar.guidance: discursive adjunct: marks quoted/spoken discourse stretch (e.g. turned and said "…")—keep as speech framing

grammar.name: Exemplificative
grammar.explanation: Indicates the word/phrase constitutes an illustrative example for the preceding formative or phrase. Translates a clause in English beginning with 'for example,...'
grammar.guidance: exemplificative adjunct: prefer 'for example, …' / 'e.g. …'

grammar.explanation: This adjunct combines the Carrier Adjunct with the discursive Register Adjunct to allow direct quotes to be placed within a case-frame, useful for translating imbedded quotes within sentences such as He told me "get out of the house!"
grammar.guidance: quotative adjunct: marks verbatim quote content (e.g. a commanded 'leave the room!')—keep quote force

grammar.name: Polyadic Animate Third Party
grammar.description: "they" — more than one animate third party

grammar.name: Mixed Animate/Inanimate Third Party
grammar.description: animate and inanimate together, e.g. "s/he and it"

grammar.name: Reduplicative
grammar.description: refers back to the party already named (resumptive)

grammar.name: Obviative
grammar.description: a third party other than the one already referenced

grammar.name: Provisional
grammar.description: "whatever" — a vague or unknown party; the case usually carries the sense

grammar.name: Neutral
grammar.description: the act has no particular benefit or harm for the referent

grammar.name: Beneficial
grammar.description: the act is to the referent's benefit

grammar.name: Detrimental
grammar.description: the act is to the referent's detriment

topics.name: observational
topics.explanation: present sensory knowledge or present sensory experience: "I perceive... / I know..."
topics.guidance: epistemic source; do not force a matrix "I perceive that…" when another party is the case-marked subject; on impersonal/eventive clauses with no case-marked actor, prefer 'takes place' / 'there's … going on' — do not add 'is observed'

topics.name: recollective
topics.explanation: past sensory knowledge or past sensory experience – "I remember... / I know (from memory)..."
topics.guidance: recollective remembered knowledge: keep as recalled fact (e.g. 'A lived longer than B…' as remembered), not newly inferred

topics.name: purportive
topics.explanation: knowledge from a definitive/(quasi-)verifiable 3rd party source: "I've read... / (an expert) has said..."
topics.guidance: purportive alleged/yet-to: prefer 'had not yet …' / purported timeline claim (e.g. 'cities had not yet formed in that era')

topics.name: reportive
topics.explanation: knowledge from a 3rd party: "I heard (from someone)... / someone has said..."
topics.guidance: reportive hearsay: prefer a hearsay matrix ('I'm told…' / 'I hear…') before the reported clause

topics.name: unspecified
topics.explanation: Validation deliberately unspecified — the speaker makes no commitment as to the epistemic source or evidentiary basis for the statement
topics.guidance: unspecified validation: no special evidential matrix—render the clause plainly (e.g. a plain milestone statement)

topics.name: imaginary
topics.explanation: unreal statement, not intended as true, based on whim, imagination, dream, altered mental state, etc.
topics.guidance: imaginary validation: treat as imagined/unreal (e.g. 'there's a dragon in the attic' as imaginary)

topics.name: intuitive
topics.explanation: intuition, hunch, subjective feeling, past experiences, etc. – "I feel... / I have a hunch... / something tells me..."
topics.guidance: When ITU validates a modal/nomic formative with ACT (no separate speaker formative), render speaker intuition with a matrix like 'I think…' (do not omit it). When a case-marked subject already carries perceptual content, omit redundant matrix 'I think/feel'.

topics.name: inferential
topics.explanation: inference from evidence (or absence of alternatives), induction, extrapolation, etc. "I infer... / I reason..."
topics.guidance: inferential must-be: prefer 'must be …' inference (e.g. 'the guests must be ready')

topics.name: directive
topics.explanation: the statement is either an imperative command to another party to do/be something, or a "commissive" statement committing the speaker to a specific state or course of action (i.e., a vow, promise, guarantee, etc.)
topics.guidance: directive command: prefer imperative to the addressee (e.g. 'Walk away from the platform!')

topics.name: declarative
topics.explanation: a "performative" statement which. by its utterance/publication, creates a change of state (at least psychologically) for the addressees (i.e., a declaration, announcement, edict, etc.)
topics.guidance: do not add a matrix 'I hereby declare that…' clause; prefer direct announcement/presentation force (e.g. 'Here's…' / 'We have…' / 'What a…!'); with compete.to.win+ACCESSOR-IND+SLF:BEN, announce the winner in 2nd/3rd-person presentation force—never 1st-person 'I declare myself the winner' / 'I've won'

topics.name: interrogative
topics.explanation: a statement whose purpose is to inquire or seek information from the addressee (i.e., equivalent to an English WH-question) -- see Sec. 10.6 for further explanation on the use of IRG Illocution
topics.guidance: interrogative content question: keep wh-question force on the queried relation/time/place

topics.name: verificative
topics.explanation: a statement whose purpose is to seek/obtain corroboration, confirmation, or verification (i.e., equivalent to a Yes/No question)
topics.guidance: verificative yes/no check: prefer a polar question seeking confirmation (e.g. 'Are the guests ready?')

topics.name: admonitive
topics.explanation: a statement whose purpose is to provide advisory/admonitive information to the addressee (i.e., a warning)
topics.guidance: admonitive warning: prefer 'Beware of …!' / warning imperative (e.g. 'Beware of thin ice!')

topics.name: potentiative
topics.explanation: a statement of wishing, hoping, or other unreal(ized) provenance
topics.guidance: when OBG (must/have to) + ACT co-occur, prefer obligation ("must") over stacking "hope" from POT

topics.name: hortative
topics.explanation: a counterfactual statement indicating a desired but impossible state of affairs that cannot be realized (equivalent to English hortative constructions such as If only..., Were that..., If only it were so that...)
topics.guidance: counterfactual wish: "If only …"; with NEG on pathogen stem + ADI illness, the wish is that the ABS party GET the disease—not that they remain not-ill

topics.name: conjectural
topics.explanation: Equivalent to an English-language "if"-clause, indicating that the statement is offered as a conjectured hypothetical, ostensibly to be followed by a "then..." implicational clause. Translatable as "If (it were the case that)..."
topics.guidance: conjectural if-then speculation: prefer 'If you …, there'll be …' conjectural consequence (e.g. 'If you enter the cave, there'll be no easy return')

topics.name: case-frame
topics.explanation: The New Ithkuil equivalent to relative or subordinate clauses is known as a case-frame, or simply, frame.
topics.guidance: case-frame: subordinate temporal/circumstantial frame for the main clause (e.g. 'After the workers finish the shift, they must …')—keep frame as adjunct, not the main predicate

topics.name: descriptive case
topics.explanation: a noun in the descriptive case, which operates like RELATIVE case for adjectival clauses
topics.guidance: descriptive case-frame: relative/descriptive clause characterizing the head (e.g. 'bird-watching hikers tend to wake early')—do not promote the frame to a main-clause only reading

topics.name: Slot V affixes
topics.explanation: Slot V affixes: If a CA complex is present in Slot VI of the formative, any Slot V affixes are shownin reversed form: -CSVX-; however, if the Slot IV VR and Slot VI CA complex have been elided as indicated by Slot I (see Sec._3.10 on "short-cut" formatives), then any Slot V affixes are shown in the standard form -VXCS-. As detailed earlier in Sec. 3.6.1, the presence of a Slot V affix requires any Slot VI CA complex to be geminated. ALSO: The semantic scope of any Slot V affixes applies only to the formative Stem, not to its Slot VI CA affix-complex (i.e., the various meanings of the CA affix-complex are applied to the formative stem AFTER the stem has first been modified by its Slot V affixes).
topics.guidance: Slot V affix string: affixes before Ca; e.g. size+configuration stacked on a stem ('a group of large but otherwise dissimilar boxes')

topics.name: Slot VII affixes
topics.explanation: Slot VII affixes are shown in standard form -VXCS- form, and apply to both the stem AND its CA affix-complex (i.e., the meanings of the CA affix-complex are applied to the formative stem first, then the resulting stem+CA complex is then modified by any Slot VII affixes). Note that in the absence of any Slot V affix(es), the presence of any Slot VII affix(es) does not trigger the gemination of any Slot VI CA complex.
topics.guidance: Slot VII affix string: affixes after Ca; e.g. quantity stacked outside configuration ('a large group of dissimilar boxes')

topics.name: purposive
topics.explanation: The entity/act/event which constitutes the inherent/innate/intrinsic purpose of another entity/act/event
topics.guidance: purposive function-as-name: English often names the tool by purpose (e.g. 'a watering can')

topics.name: Type-1
topics.explanation: Type-1 case-accessor affix for ergative case
topics.guidance: Type-1 ergative accessor: circumstantial agent — prefer 'the party who did X' / 'whoever caused X' (not a lexicalized role noun yet)

topics.name: Type-2
topics.explanation: Type-2 case-accessor affix for ergative case
topics.guidance: Type-2 ergative accessor: prefer a lexicalized agent noun when English has one (perpetrator/culprit/author)—not a bare relative 'who did…'

topics.name: Type-1
topics.explanation: Type-1 case-accessor affix for productive case
topics.guidance: Type-1 productive accessor: circumstantial creator — prefer 'the one who designed/produced X'

topics.name: Type-2
topics.explanation: Type-2 case-accessor affix for productive case
topics.guidance: Type-2 productive accessor: prefer a lexicalized creator noun (architect/author/composer of X) when English has one

topics.name: Type-1
topics.explanation: Type-1 case-accessor affix for compositive case
topics.guidance: Type-1 compositive accessor: circumstantial material — prefer 'what X is made out of'

topics.name: Type-2
topics.explanation: Type-2 case-accessor affix for compositive case
topics.guidance: Type-2 compositive accessor: prefer a lexicalized materials NP ('X's construction materials' / 'X's makeup')

topics.name: Type-1
topics.explanation: Type-1 inverse case-accessor affix for comitative case
topics.guidance: Type-1 comitative accessor: circumstantial companion — prefer 'the one whom Y is with'

topics.name: Type-2
topics.explanation: Type-2 inverse case-accessor affix for comitative case
topics.guidance: Type-2 comitative accessor: prefer a lexicalized companion role (chaperone/escort/companion) when English has one

topics.name: Type-1
topics.explanation: Type-1 inverse case-accessor affix for ergative case
topics.guidance: Type-1 inverse ergative accessor: what the absolutive party did to the ergative party — prefer 'what A did to B'

topics.name: Type-3
topics.explanation: Type-3 case-accessor affix for instrumental case
topics.guidance: Type-3 instrumental accessor: instrument/means nominal scoped via Type-3 (e.g. 'that by which a calm outcome occurs')—not the stem alone

topics.name: Type-3 inverse case-accessor
topics.explanation: Type-3 inverse case-accessor affix for instrumental case
topics.guidance: Type-3 inverse instrumental accessor: what the instrument is used for (e.g. 'what a calm outcome is used for')

topics.name: Type-3
topics.explanation: Type-3 case-accessor affix for ergative case
topics.guidance: nominal ergative agent of the stem: with upward.motion+DNG, agent who pushes (dangerously) upward—not the figure that merely moves upward

topics.name: Type-3 inverse case-accessor
topics.explanation: Type-3 inverse case-accessor affix for ergative case
topics.guidance: Type-3 inverse ergative accessor: patient/figure of the Type-3-scoped agentive act (e.g. 'that which one carefully lifts upward')

topics.name: Type-3
topics.explanation: Type-3 case-accessor affix for purposive case
topics.guidance: nominal purposive referent: with interfere+AUT, prefer a nominal 'purpose for [authorized interference]'—not adverbial 'for the purpose of…'

topics.name: Type-3 inverse case-accessor
topics.explanation: Type-3 inverse case-accessor affix for purposive case
topics.guidance: Type-3 inverse purposive accessor: purpose-of reading inverted (e.g. 'what using careful authority to intervene is for')

topics.name: conversive
topics.explanation: Case-stacking affix used with conversive case; using the case-stacking affix on unframed verbal formatives can function as a substitute for case-frames
topics.guidance: conversive exception: prefer 'except X' / 'all but X' (e.g. 'everything was packed except the lamp')

topics.name: ordering of the formatives
topics.explanation: ordering of formatives, placement of case-stacking affix, and use of TPF affix
topics.guidance: formative order/case-stacking: keep stacked modifiers aligned to the intended head (e.g. looking at a book about capturing animals)—do not reassign the about-clause to the wrong noun

topics.name: single-affix
topics.explanation: This adjunct associates a single VXCS affix to the following formative and provides scoping information over the formative's other VXCS affixes. The tell-tale sign of this adjunct is the V-C-(V) form containing only one full consonant-form. Examples: ač, iakse, etra, usmú, aull.
topics.guidance: single-affix adjunct: one VxCs affix only; keep that single modification (e.g. hurry alone → 'in a hurry')

topics.name: multiple-affix
topics.explanation: associates two or more affixes to a formative
topics.guidance: multiple-affix adjunct: stacked affixes; keep all stacked senses (e.g. timing+avoidance together → 'just in time to avoid …')

topics.name: modular
topics.explanation: has two slots corresponding to formative Slot VIII showing Valence, Phase, Level, or Effect, in combination with Mood/Case-Scope, or showing Aspect plus Mood/Case-Scope
topics.guidance: modular adjunct: mood/module bundle; keep modality+aspectual pieces (e.g. might + resume + random bursts)

topics.name: Type-2 Concatenation
topics.explanation: Type-2 concatenation is derivational (i.e., lexicalizing), creating a new lexico-semantic gestalt usually requiring a different English translation.
topics.guidance: derivational concatenation: ROOT-'person'+child context often yields 'child' (not bare 'person'); prefer the lexicalized English reading
